name: Pomelo
summary: This guide shows how Filipino growers usually plant pomelo from a marcot or grafted seedling and care for it until it bears fruit worth selling. It is for backyards and small orchards, such as the Magallanes pomelo farms of Davao.
season: Marcots and seedlings are planted as the rains begin, around May to July, so they root before the dry months. In Davao and other places where rain spreads through the year, planting goes on in most wet months.
material: Most growers plant a marcot (air layer) taken from a heavy bearing tree with sweet, juicy fruit, or a grafted seedling on a hardy rootstock. Some growers prefer big marcots, over 1.5 m tall, because they survive well and may give a few fruits within a year. Trees grown from seed take long to bear and the fruit can differ from the mother tree.
spacing: About 8 to 10 m between trees, often 10 m by 10 m, or 8 to 10 m between rows and 6 to 8 m in the row. Holes about 50 cm wide and deep, one plant a hole.
water: Mostly rain fed. New trees are watered every few days in dry weather and mulched. Growers who can water during flowering and fruit growth in dry spells get better fruit set.
fertilizer: Compost or dried manure in the hole at planting. Young trees get a little complete fertilizer or ammonium sulfate (21 0 0) every three to four months, more each year. Bearing trees get fertilizer with more potash, plus micronutrients, at the start and end of the rains. Growers note that the wrong feeding gives thick rind and dry, bland flesh.
care: Staking, mulching and weeding around young trees, light pruning to remove water sprouts, dead twigs and branches that touch the ground, and heavier pruning right after the main harvest. Thinning fruits that come in clusters so the rest grow big. Checking new flushes for aphids and psyllids and the trunk for gum. Many growers bag the young fruits against fruit flies and rind borers.
harvest: Pomelo needs no flower inducer and can give a main crop and a smaller off season crop each year. Fruit is picked when full sized, with lighter colored, smooth, shiny skin, by cutting the stem rather than pulling. The fruit keeps a month or more in a cool, shaded place, and is handled gently so the rind does not bruise.

ways.label: Marcot or grafted seedling (marcot o grafted)

steps.title: Make your own marcots (pagmamarcot)
steps.how: Growers who have a sweet, juicy, heavy bearing tree often root their own marcots on it in the rainy months. Some prefer big marcots, since they survive well in the field.

parts.title: Choose the mother tree and the branch
parts.how: Pick a tree that bears every year, with good fruit and no pests or disease, and not too old. On it choose a branch about as thick as a finger or a little more, neither too young nor too old, growing upward in the sun, with no flowers or fruit on it.

parts.title: Mix the rooting ball
parts.how: Mix garden soil with rice hull, or with mudpress from a sugar mill or coir dust where you can get it. Wet it until it holds together when squeezed but does not drip.

parts.title: Peel a ring of bark
parts.how: With a clean, sharp knife, cut twice around the branch a short distance apart and peel off the bark between the cuts. Scrape off the slippery green layer under the bark too, or the bark heals over instead of making roots.

parts.title: Wrap and tie
parts.how: Hold a piece of clear plastic around the branch below the ring, pack a ball of the moist mix over the whole ring, close the plastic around it and tie both ends tightly with plastic straw.

parts.title: Wait for the roots
parts.how: Leave the wrap on the tree and look at it every week or two. The marcot is ready when white roots show plainly all around the ball through the plastic. If the ball dries, open the top and add a little water.

parts.title: Cut it and bag it
parts.how: Cut the branch just below the ball with sharp shears or a saw. Take off the plastic gently, without breaking the ball, and plant it in a 6 by 8 inch bag of two parts soil, one part compost and one part rice hull.

parts.title: Nurse it in the shade
parts.how: Keep the new plant in the shade, out of the rain, and water it daily. After two weeks move it where it gets some sun, and pick off any flowers so it grows roots and leaves first.
parts.tip: A big marcot needs a bigger bag or pot than the 6 by 8 inch size, so its roots are not cramped.

steps.title: Clear the land and mark the spots
steps.how: Clear the land and mark the planting spots about 8 to 10 m apart, since pomelo grows into a big tree. Pick ground that drains well. On slopes follow the contour.

steps.title: Dig and fill the holes
steps.how: Dig each hole about 50 cm wide and 50 cm deep and keep the topsoil apart. Mix the topsoil with compost or dried manure and put it back to settle before planting.

steps.title: Pick and harden the marcot
steps.how: Choose a marcot or grafted seedling with plenty of roots, healthy dark leaves and no gum on the bark. Keep it in light shade and water it daily for some days so it gets used to the field.

steps.title: Plant and stake
steps.how: Remove the bag or wrapping without breaking the soil ball and set the plant at the depth it grew. Firm the soil, water well and tie the plant to a strong stake against the wind.

steps.title: Shade, mulch and water
steps.how: Shade the new tree with fronds for a few weeks and mulch around it, a little away from the stem. Water every few days in dry weather until new leaves show.

steps.title: First feeding
steps.how: About a month after planting, spread a small amount of complete fertilizer or ammonium sulfate around the tree and mix it lightly into the soil. Feed again every three to four months, a little more each year, with manure when you have it.

steps.title: Weed around the young tree
steps.how: Keep a clean circle around the tree by hand or bolo. Short crops can be grown between the young trees.

steps.title: Check new leaves and bark
steps.how: Look at each new flush for aphids, psyllids and leaf miners, and at the trunk for gum oozing from the bark. Cut and burn badly hit twigs and keep the base dry and clean.

steps.title: Shape the young tree
steps.how: Cut back the tips to make the tree branch, keep a few strong main branches and remove water sprouts and branches that touch the ground. Pick off early fruits so the tree builds its frame first.

steps.title: Feed more as the tree grows
steps.how: From the second year, feed the tree at the start and the end of the rains, spreading the fertilizer under the outer leaves. Bearing trees need more potash for sweet, juicy fruit.

steps.title: First good harvest
steps.how: Pick when the fruit is full sized, the skin turns lighter green or yellowish and the oil glands look smooth and shiny. Cut the stem with a pruning knife or a pole cutter so the fruit does not drop.

ways.note: A pomelo tree gives enough fruit to sell at about 4 years from planting. Big marcots may give a few fruits in the first year or two.

mistakes: Planting seedlings from seed, which bear late and give fruits unlike the mother tree.
Taking marcots from a sour or poor bearing tree.
Planting too close, so the big trees shade each other.
Letting every fruit in a cluster grow, so all stay small.
Giving the wrong fertilizer, which gives thick rind and dry flesh.
Leaving fruit flies and rind borers unchecked in the orchard.
better: Buy marcots or grafted seedlings from an accredited nursery or a proven mother tree.
Test the soil and feed by the result, with enough potash and micronutrients.
Prune right after the main harvest and thin fruit clusters.
Bag young fruits and keep fallen fruit cleaned up against fruit flies and rind borers.
Water during flowering and fruit growth in long dry spells.
Scout every new flush for aphids and psyllids that spread citrus diseases.

watering.traditional: Pomelo here is mostly rain fed: a new marcot is watered every few days in dry weather and mulched, then left to the rain. Growers who can water during flowering and fruit growth in the dry months get a better fruit set and a second, off season crop.
watering.method: A pail or hose into a ring basin under the edge of the leaves on small farms. Drip lines or small sprinklers on the bigger orchards in Mindanao and Luzon. Water early in the morning.
watering.rainfed: Plant as the rains begin, stake the marcot against wind, and mulch a little away from the trunk. Mulch again before the dry months. On slopes, plant along the contour with a small basin on the downhill side of each tree. Rain fed trees give their main crop on the rains and little off season fruit.
watering.dryseason: First year: every 3 to 4 days. Second year: every 3 to 7 days, by soil. Bearing trees: every 5 to 10 days through flowering and fruit growth. Water when leaves curl and lose their shine by midday, or when small fruits start to drop.
watering.wet: Wet soil against the trunk brings gum oozing from the bark and root rot, the trouble that ruins many pomelo farms here. Keep the base dry and clean, never pile soil or mulch on the trunk, water the ring under the leaves, and plant on ground that drains well with open drains from low spots.

schedule.often: Every day for the week before planting, in light shade
schedule.amount: Enough to wet the soil ball right through
schedule.why: A marcot has a small, shallow root ball that dries out in hours.

schedule.often: Soak on planting day, then every 2 to 3 days in dry weather until new leaves show
schedule.amount: Half to one watering can a tree each time, into a ring basin away from the stem
schedule.why: The new roots have to grow out of the marcot ball into the field.

schedule.often: Every 3 to 4 days in the dry months. Not needed in steady rain
schedule.amount: One watering can a tree each time, or about 1 to 5 liters a tree a day on drip
schedule.why: Marcotted trees have no deep tap root and feel a dry spell sooner than seedlings.

schedule.often: Every 3 to 4 days on light soil and about once a week on clay, in the dry months
schedule.amount: About 3 to 5 watering cans a tree each time, or 10 to 15 liters a tree a day on drip
schedule.why: Each new flush builds the wide crown a pomelo needs.

schedule.often: Every 4 to 7 days in the dry months
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the whole ring under the leaves, or about 15 to 40 liters a tree a day on drip as it grows
schedule.why: Big marcots may fruit early. Pick those fruits off and keep the tree growing.

schedule.stage: Bearing trees: short dry spell before flowering (each year)
schedule.often: Let the soil get drier for a few weeks late in the dry months, then soak deeply with the fertilizer
schedule.amount: Little or none for a few weeks, then one deep soak
schedule.why: Like other citrus, pomelo flowers when water returns after a dry spell.

schedule.often: Every 5 to 7 days in dry weather, never letting the soil dry out
schedule.amount: A deep soak of the ring under the leaves, out to the edge of the crown
schedule.why: Dry soil now drops the flowers and the young fruits.

schedule.often: Every 7 to 10 days in dry spells
schedule.amount: A deep soak under the crown
schedule.why: Steady water gives big, juicy fruits with a thinner rind.

schedule.often: Water lightly and evenly. Avoid one heavy flood after a long dry spell
schedule.amount: A normal soak of the ring
schedule.why: A sudden flood after dry weeks can split ripening fruits.

critical: The first year after planting, since a marcot has shallow roots.
Flowering and fruit set, when dry soil drops flowers and young fruits.
Fruit growth in the dry months, which decides fruit size and juice.

signs.dry: Leaves curl and fold along the middle, lose their shine, and older ones yellow and fall. New flushes stop and small fruits drop.
signs.wet: Leaves yellow all over, gum oozes from the trunk, roots rot, and branches die back.

better: Drip or a mulched ring basin watered through the dry months lets the tree carry an off season crop, when pomelo sells best.
Keep the soil steadily moist from flowering through fruit set and keep water off the trunk to cut fruit drop and gum.
